title: LatentRouter: Can We Choose the Right Multimodal Large Language Model Before Seeing Its Answer?
claim: A router scores each candidate by iteratively exchanging information between query states and model states, then invokes only the best one.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right, numbered sub-stages, operator legend along bottom
description: A wide three-panel diagram. Panel (a), on the left, shows how states are built. A chart-question query, "Which month has the highest sales?", goes through cross-attention to produce orange routing capsules R(0). Below it, blue model capability tokens A(0) are built from model metadata: calibration profile, mean cost, latency and local statistics, combined by a projection. Panel (b), in the middle, has three stacked boxes repeated for H rounds: model-conditioned attention, pairwise communication with masked self-attention, and decision-aware feedback. Panel (c), on the right, has three stacked boxes: distributional outcome prediction, bounded capsule correction, and a routing policy with the utility formula s_i = μ_i + Δ_i^cap − λĉ_i. That policy picks the selected model m*, which produces the answer. Orange marks capsules and blue marks tokens. A legend of operator icons runs along the bottom.
caption: Overview of LatentRouter. (a) Multimodal routing capsules encode the image--question query, while model capability tokens combine model metadata and query-specific calibration statistics. (b) Over $H$ rounds, model-conditioned attention, availability-masked pairwise communication, and decision-aware feedback iteratively update the two sets of states. (c) A shared outcome head predicts each model's counterfactual answer-quality distribution. A bounded capsule correction refines the predicted mean, and the routing policy selects the available model with the highest cost-adjusted utility. Only the selected MLLM is invoked to generate an answer. Orange and blue denote routing capsules and model capability tokens, respectively.
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have heterogeneous strengths across OCR, chart understanding, spatial reasoning, visual question answering, cost, and latency. Effective MLLM routing therefore requires more than estimating query difficulty: a router must match the multimodal requirements of the current image-question input with the capabilities of each candidate model. We propose LatentRouter, a router that formulates MLLM routing as counterfactual multimodal utility prediction. Given an image-question query, LatentRouter extracts learned multimodal routing capsules, represents each candidate MLLM with a model capability token, and performs latent communication between these states to estimate how each model would perform if selected. A distributional outcome head predicts model-specific counterfactual quality, while a bounded capsule correction refines close decisions without allowing residual signals to dominate the prediction. The resulting utility-based policy supports performance-oriented and performance-cost routing, and handles changing candidate pools through shared per-model scoring with availability masking. Experiments on MMR-Bench and VL-RouterBench show that LatentRouter outperforms fixed-model, feature-level, and learned-router baselines. Additional analyses show that the gains are strongest on multimodal task groups where model choice depends on visual, layout-sensitive, or reasoning-oriented requirements, and that latent communication is the main contributor to the improvement. The code is available at: https://github.com/LabRAI/LatentRouter.
